kicker: Hotrod Outdoor Alaska Fishing · update report
title: Climbing, Tesla, science and a visitor from the sky
lede: Everything from your last message is in the game: the iPhone fixes, rock climbing at the Granite Tors, a Tesla memorial at Bear Falls, 23 science objectives, and a meteor shower that brings down a small companion called Zib.

sections.title: What you asked for, and where it stands
sections.html:
Every point in your message, in the order you wrote it. The first four went out in the earlier commit 524a864; the other four are new in this round.

#You askedWhat changedStatus
1On iPhone in landscape the RUN button sits in the small mapOn short screens RUN now sits beside the small map instead of on it. The action buttons, first aid and bear spray keep clear of each other and of the top buttons, and the horn and camera sit above the pedals. Checked for overlaps at ten screen sizes, walking and driving.Done (524a864)
2The voice that says “fish on” sounds like a robotThe announcer no longer uses Fred, Apple’s robot voice, pitched down. It picks the most natural English voice on the device (enhanced and premium voices first, never a novelty voice) and speaks at that voice’s own pitch. Settings has a Voice button to hear and pick another.Done (524a864). How natural it sounds depends on the voices installed on the phone
3The buttons in the top right do nothing when tappedThe wardrobe, map, journal and pause buttons and the small map now act when the finger lifts over them, instead of waiting for the browser’s click. iOS drops that click when a tap wobbles while the game is taking touches. A finger that starts on a button no longer has its moves cancelled.Done (524a864); not yet tried on a real iPhone
4Very laggy at timesThree causes of hitches removed. The sky’s reflection map reuses one render target instead of making a new one every few seconds at dusk, and is not redrawn deep in the night. The forest’s rebuild after a turn is spread over several frames. The automatic resolution no longer steps up and down every few seconds.Done (524a864); the frame rate on a real phone was not measured here
5Rock climbing that fits the themeThe Granite Tors: two towers of granite on a meadow off the Tundra Road, with four top-rope routes climbed hold by hold.Done
6A statue of Nikola TeslaThe Tesla Memorial at Bear Falls: a sculpted bronze Tesla, seated and reading, after the statue on Goat Island at Niagara Falls. Beside it are a working Tesla coil and the falls’ hydro plant.Done
7General science objectives in the quests23 science objectives in five fields, a new Science page in the Journal, and three science odd jobs.Done
8A telescope event: meteor shower, a flying object crashing within reach, a friendly odd alien companionA meteor outburst seen through the telescope. Among the meteors a craft falls, burning, and crashes about 700 m from the observatory. At the crash site is Zib, a small three-eyed creature that can come along as your companion.Done

sections.title: Buttons that answer, a layout that fits, a natural voice
sections.html:
These went out in the commit before this round. They are repeated here so the whole message is answered in one place.

  • Buttons. The four round buttons in the top right and the small map listen for the finger lifting over them (touchend), not for the browser’s click. Safari does not send a click when the finger moves a little during the tap, and the game was taking that touch for looking around. That is why nothing happened.
  • Layout. On a phone on its side under Safari’s bars the screen is only about 330 points tall. RUN now sits to the right of the small map, and the other buttons were moved so that nothing overlaps. A script checked every pair of buttons for overlap at ten screen sizes, walking and driving.
  • Voice. The old announcer used the voice called Fred, pitched down, which is what made it sound like a robot. It now ranks the voices on the device, with enhanced and premium voices first and the novelty voices left out. In Settings, tap Voice to hear the next voice and keep the one you like. On an iPhone, better voices can be downloaded in Settings → Accessibility → Spoken Content → Voices → English.
  • Lag. The sky’s reflection map used to be thrown away and rebuilt every few seconds while the light changed. Each rebuild was a large memory allocation and a visible hitch at dusk. Now one target is made once and reused, refreshed every 4 degrees of the sun’s movement and at most every 5 seconds, and not at all deep in the night. The forest’s rebuild after a turn is spread over frames. The automatic resolution waits longer each time a step up has to be taken back, so it no longer stutters up and down.

sections.title: The Granite Tors
sections.html:
Two towers of granite stand on a meadow off the Tundra Road, like the tors in the hills near Fairbanks. A tor is what is left standing when the weaker rock round a body of granite weathers away. Frost opens the joints into stacked blocks and rounds their corners. The big tor is four blocks high and the little one two. The Kenai Climbing Club keeps four top ropes on them, each in its own colour. The Trading Post sells a climbing kit (rock shoes, a harness and a chalk bag) for $140. On a top rope the rope runs from your harness up to the anchor and back down, so a slip is a short drop onto the rope, not a fall.

How it plays

  • Push the stick (or the arrow keys) toward the next hold, or tap a hold, and the hand that can reach it goes there.
  • Every hold tires your fingers at its own rate: a jug least, then an edge, a pocket and a sloper, and a crimp most. The steeper the rock, the faster: an overhang drains three times as fast as a slab.
  • CHALK dries your fingers and buys back some grip. A big hold on rock that is not overhanging lets you rest, and the grip meter then reads REST.
  • Run out of grip and you come off. The rope holds you, and you can CLIMB ON when you have your breath back or LOWER OFF to the ground.
  • At the top you stand on the tor with the view. Sign the register, take the geologist’s granite sample from the big tor, and LOWER OFF from the anchor.
  • Two new challenges: climb any route ($250) and climb Raven’s Roof ($600).

The routes

RouteGradeWhereHoldsHeight
First Steps5.4The little tor, south-west facejugs 70 %, edges 30 %6.3 m
Tundra Stroll5.5The big tor, south facejugs 50 %, edges 42 %, slopers 8 %15.2 m
Ptarmigan Crack5.8The big tor, north face, up a crackedges 42 %, jugs 24 %, pockets 17 %, crimps 17 %13.9 m
Raven’s Roof5.10The big tor, east face, under the overhangcrimps 34 %, edges 24 %, slopers 20 %, pockets 12 %, jugs 10 %15.4 m

The grades are the American ones. “5” means a climb that needs a rope, and the number after the point says how hard it is. The holds are chalked white, as they are on real crags.

Problems found by climbing every route, and fixed

  • Raven’s Roof stalled at a ledge where the next hold was 1.5 m away. Holds are now spaced by distance over the rock, not by height, so ledges and the roof get as many holds as a flat face.
  • The roof then drained the grip to nothing. Big holds on rock that is not overhanging now let you rest, a move costs less, and a big hold sits just past the lip of the roof (the kind climbers call a thank-god jug).
  • After a fall under the roof the climber could not get back on. CLIMB ON now looks for holds near where you came off.
  • The tors cost 466 draw calls. Merging each tor’s blocks into one mesh and all the ropes into another brought that down to 276.

sections.title: The Tesla Memorial at Bear Falls
sections.html:
Tesla (1856–1943) worked out the alternating current system that the world’s power grids still run on. The first big power station built on it was at Niagara Falls, and it sent its power to Buffalo in November 1896. Since 1976 a bronze Tesla by the sculptor Frano Kršinić, a gift from Yugoslavia, has sat on Goat Island by those falls, seated and reading his notes. The game’s memorial copies that pose. It stands on a stone terrace at the rim of the gorge at Bear Falls, above the falls’ own little hydro plant.

What is there

  • The statue on a granite base with a bronze plaque. The plaque gives his life, the rotating magnetic field of 1888, the Niagara power of 1896, his coil of 1891, and the tesla, the unit of magnetic field strength named after him in 1960. Reading it completes the science objective “The man who lit the world”.
  • The coil house: an open pavilion with a Tesla coil in an earthed wire cage. Run it and sparks crack inside the cage while a fluorescent tube on a stand lights up with no wire to it, as Tesla showed in New York on 20 May 1891. Science objective: “Light without wires”.
  • Bear Falls Hydro: the intake above the falls, a tunnel, the penstock (the big pipe) along the foot of the gorge, the powerhouse at the water with its outflow foaming back into the river, and three wires up the gorge on poles. Three wires carry three-phase alternating current, Tesla’s polyphase system. A board at the rim works out the plant’s power from the real drop measured in the game world: 1000 kg/m³ × 9.81 m/s² × 2.6 m³/s × 14.0 m × 0.85 ≈ 304 kW. That is about as much as 250 homes use on average, taking a home as about 1.2 kW (10,791 kWh a year). Science objective: “Power from falling water”.

How the statue is made

The first attempt, built from boxes and cylinders, looked like a toy. The statue is now sculpted the way a digital sculptor works: the head, the hands and the body (the coat with its lapels, the waistcoat, the collar and cravat, the coat tails falling over the chair) are smooth shapes blended into one another, written as distance fields and turned into a mesh. The result has 43,954 triangles. Building it is spread over many frames, a few milliseconds at a time, starting when you come within 1 km, so it never stalls the game. The same sculpting code (src/util/sdfmesh.js) also makes Zib.

sections.title: 23 things to see, do and find out
sections.html:
The science objectives run beside the challenges, in any order and all at once. Each one pays a reward, $3,810 in all, and keeps what you learned on the Journal’s new Science page. When you complete one, a message tells you what you learned. They are built on things already in the game (the telescope, the radio dish, the race car, the paraglider, the glacier, the hot springs, the fish, the bears and the eagles) and on the new sites. Below is every objective, with exactly what it teaches.

FieldObjectiveWhat to doWhat you learnReward
AstronomyCraters on the MoonLook at the Moon through the telescope at the Tundra ObservatoryThe craters are scars of asteroids and comets that hit the Moon. With no air or water to wear them away they last for billions of years; the dark plains are old lava flows.$120
AstronomyA planet's discSee a planet through the telescope (it finds the bright ones in daylight too)Planets shine by sunlight they reflect, and a telescope shows each one as a little disc. Stars stay points of light however much you magnify them: they are much too far away.$150
AstronomyAnother galaxyFind the Andromeda Galaxy (M31) through the telescope on a dark nightThe light you see left Andromeda about 2.5 million years ago, before there were people. It is a spiral of hundreds of billions of stars, and it is coming toward our own galaxy, the Milky Way.$200
AstronomyA dead star's heartbeatListen to a pulsar with the observatory's radio dishA pulsar is the core left when a big star explodes: a ball of neutrons about 20 km across, spinning, sweeping a beam of radio waves past the Earth like a lighthouse, from about once a second to hundreds of times a second.$180
AstronomyThe Big Bang's afterglowTune the radio dish to the cosmic microwave backgroundMicrowaves from when the universe was 380,000 years old fill the whole sky. The universe has stretched so much since that they have cooled to 2.7 degrees above absolute zero.$220
AstronomyA station in orbitWatch the International Space Station pass over (the observatory board knows when)The station goes round the Earth about every 90 minutes, 400 km up. It is falling all the time, but moving sideways so fast, about 28,000 km an hour, that it keeps missing the ground.$150
AstronomyThe northern lightsSee the aurora: a clear night, away from lights, looking northParticles from the Sun, steered by the Earth's magnetic field, rain into the air 100 to 300 km up near the poles. Oxygen there glows green and red; nitrogen glows blue and purple.$150
AstronomyA meteor showerWatch a meteor shower through the telescope (late on a clear night, when the board says one is on)A shower comes when the Earth crosses the trail of dust a comet left behind. The meteors seem to fly out of one point, the radiant, because the grains travel side by side, like snow in a car's headlights.$250
AstronomyA stone from spaceFind a meteorite where a fireball came downA meteor is the streak of light; a meteorite is the stone that reaches the ground. Most are pieces of asteroids, older than any rock on Earth: about 4.6 billion years.$200
AstronomyHow big space isWalk the solar system: all 9 signs of the scale model on the Lighthouse RoadAt the model’s scale the Sun is a ball 19 cm across and the Earth a grain 1.7 mm across, 20 m away; Neptune is 600 m down the road. The nearest star would be about 5,400 km away.$150
Physics and engineeringThe man who lit the worldRead Nikola Tesla's plaque at the memorial by Bear FallsTwo or more alternating currents, each a little behind the other, make a magnetic field that turns by itself. Tesla’s induction motor and his three-phase system still drive most of the world’s machines.$100
Physics and engineeringLight without wiresRun the Tesla coil in the coil house at Bear FallsTwo coils tuned to the same frequency pass energy back and forth and build up a very high voltage. The quickly changing field lights a gas-filled tube with no wire to it.$150
Physics and engineeringPower from falling waterRead the Bear Falls Hydro board at the rim of the gorgePower = water’s density × gravity × flow × drop × efficiency. Bear Falls’ 14 m drop and 2.6 m³ of water a second make about 300 kW, as much as about 250 homes use.$120
Physics and engineeringThe wall of airReach 250 km/h in the race car hidden in the forestAir pushes back harder the faster you go: drag grows with the square of the speed, and the power to beat it with the cube. Twice as fast takes eight times the power.$200
Physics and engineeringFlying on a wingFly Gus's paraglider off a high edgeA wing tilted to the air turns the passing air downward, and pushing air down pushes the wing up. Rising warm air, a thermal, can carry you higher than where you started.$150
Earth scienceHow granite is madeTake a rock sample on top of the big Granite TorGranite cooled slowly from molten rock deep underground, so its crystals had time to grow big enough to see: pink feldspar, grey quartz and black mica. Tors stand where frost and water stripped away the weaker rock round them.$150
Earth scienceA glacier calvingWatch the glacier drop ice into Glacier LakeA glacier is snow pressed into ice over a century or more, flowing downhill under its own weight. Where it meets water its front cracks and falls in. The lake is milky blue with rock the ice has ground to flour.$150
Earth scienceHot water from the deepSoak in the hot pool at Steaming SpringsRain and snowmelt sink through cracks in the rock, are heated by hot rock kilometres down and rise again along a fault. The deeper the water goes, the hotter it comes back.$100
BiologyThe salmon's journeyCatch a Pacific salmon: a sockeye, king, coho, pink or chumSalmon hatch in fresh water, grow up at sea and swim back to the stream they were born in, finding it by smell, to spawn once and die. Their bodies feed the bears, the eagles and the forest itself.$100
BiologyA fat bearPhotograph a bear (from a safe distance)A grizzly can eat dozens of salmon a day in late summer, building up the fat it lives on through the five or more months of its winter sleep.$150
BiologyBirds of the northPhotograph a bald eagleBald eagles gather on Alaska’s rivers when the salmon run. Their nests, used year after year, can weigh more than a tonne.$120
Life beyond EarthA visitor from the skyFind out what came down after the meteor showerLife as we know it needs liquid water, a source of energy and carbon chemistry. Astronomers have found thousands of planets round other stars, and look for ones at the right distance from their star for water to stay liquid.$300
Life beyond EarthLife at the edgesTake your companion from the sky to the hot pool at Steaming SpringsMicrobes live in boiling springs, in Antarctic ice and in rock kilometres down. If life manages here, it might on Mars under the ground, or in the ocean under the ice of Jupiter’s moon Europa.$250

Three science odd jobs

Who asksWhat forReward
A geologist from the university in FairbanksA chip of granite from the top of the big tor, to date the rock$280
Dr. Okafor at the Tundra ObservatoryA two-star picture of the Moon for the school star night$240
The weather service in AnchorageA picture of the northern lights, to check its aurora forecasts$320

To make the objectives reachable, the game now also reports a paraglider launch, a glacier calving, a strong aurora overhead at night and a rock sample, and it notes whether Zib was with you in the hot pool.

sections.title: A visitor from the sky
sections.html:
1. The forecast. From the start of the game the Tundra Observatory’s Tonight board lists a meteor outburst: the Kappa Cygnids, out of Cygnus high overhead. On the first clear evening, between 21:24 and 23:30, a message says it is on.
  2. The sky. While the night is dark and clear, slow meteors streak across the real sky every few seconds, all out of the radiant in Cygnus.
  3. The telescope. The telescope has a new target, Meteor outburst. It shows an animated wide-field view with meteors flying out of the radiant. Then comes a light that is far too slow, and turns. The panel beside it explains the shower, and watching completes the objective “A meteor shower”.
  4. The fall. Step back outside and the craft comes down over 11 seconds, glowing with the heat of the air it rams and trailing smoke. It lands in the forest about 700 m from the observatory. There is a flash, and the boom arrives 2 seconds later, because sound covers only about 343 m a second.
  5. Starfall Clearing. The crash site goes on the map, with a parking place on the River Road about 110 m away, so the map’s Drive there takes you close. The trees round the pod lie flat, pointing outward, as they did round the blast at Tunguska in 1908. The ground is scorched, the hull cools over the first hours and the smoke thins over two days.
  6. Zib. Something hides behind the pod and peeks out when you come close. SAY HELLO: it chirps three notes, you clap back, and then its ears flash the prime numbers, two, three, five, seven, eleven. Then you can invite it along or let it rest there.
  7. The companion. Zib floats at your shoulder and rides in the hot rod’s passenger seat and in the boat. Its mood shows that a fish is coming before the bite, and it squeaks when a bear is near. It waits where you ask it to and blinks back to you if you get far away. A three-star picture of Zib sells to the magazine for $250. Take it to the hot pool at Steaming Springs to complete “Life at the edges”.

The site’s first name, “The crash site”, clashed with an older oddity in the woods, a crashed saucer. The new clearing is now Starfall Clearing.

In its place the panel describes the shower’s seven-year cycle, its slow golden meteors and its flaring fireballs, and names the other proposed parent bodies.
  • Space station: “7.7 km a second” is now “about 28,000 km an hour”, the figure the source gives (the two are the same speed).
  • Glacier: snow is pressed into glacier ice “over a century or more”, not “over hundreds of years”.

sections.title: What the new sites cost to draw
sections.html:
Draw calls and triangles are counted in the game’s own renderer, standing at each site and looking at it. The headless test browser draws with software at about 4 seconds a frame, so it cannot show the frame rate. These counts are what decides the frame rate on a phone.

PlaceDraw callsTriangles
Hotrod Landing, for comparison2611.27 million
Tesla Memorial2951.42 million
Starfall Clearing, with the fall’s light still in the sky3381.27 million
Granite Tors (466 draw calls before their blocks and ropes were merged)2861.33 million

Measured on the final build. The counts move by a few per cent with the view, the time of day and what the forest has loaded.

  • The statue has 43,954 triangles. On the final build it is sculpted over 111 frames, at most 3 ms of work in a frame, 386 ms of work in all. The longest single step, the very first, took 9 ms while the browser compiled the code. Zib takes 19 frames and 62 ms.
  • Zib is sculpted the same way, a little each frame, when you first come near it. The statue and Zib share one budget of 3 ms a frame, so near the crash site, 255 m from the memorial, the two never add up.
  • The falling craft’s trail is two point clouds, one of glow and one of smoke: two draw calls where it was up to about 100 at the climax.
  • Rays against the tors (placing the holds, lowering off) test one block at a time, and lowering off casts one every 0.1 s.
  • The blocks of each tor are one mesh, and all the ropes and rope coils are one more.
  • Grass is cleared from under the terrace, the coil house and the crash site, so it no longer grows through the stone and the scorched ground.

sections.title: What the review found, and what was fixed
sections.html:
A separate review agent read every new file of this round against the rest of the game. It then ran the game in the headless browser to confirm what it could. It reported 17 findings, and all 17 are fixed. Two more turned up while this report was being written. “Run in the game” means a test script checked the fix: tools/scenarios/review-fixes.json, plus the other scripts listed under Tests. The review also found that the headless browser only draws a frame when a picture is taken, which is why the scripts step the game themselves.

SeverityFindingWhat went wrongFixChecked
HighZib left behind after a fast travelWith Zib along, a fast travel left it 867 m behind and out of sight. It only moved while within 600 m of the camera. That also blocked “Life at the edges” after a fast travel to the springs.A companion who is with you always keeps up: far off, it blinks to your side.Run in the game: 1.4 m from you after the travel
HighFast travel while climbingThe map’s Drive there still worked on the rope. The hot rod drove off and the hours passed, and the next frame put you back on the route.Refused while climbing, on the map and in the travel itself: “Lower off first: you are on the rope”.Run in the game: refused, no time passed, still on the route
MediumObjectives an older save could never completeThe telescope, the radio dish, the camera, the solar system’s signs, the race car’s speed marks and the aurora report a thing only the first time. A player who had done them before this update could never complete their objectives.On loading, the save’s logs are read, those objectives are credited and paid, and a message lists them.Run in the game: a test save with old logs got 10 objectives and $1,520, with the message
MediumDrive there to Starfall Clearing did nothingThe clearing had no parking place, so the travel quietly stopped. It was also never marked as discovered, so the map hid its name.A parking place on the River Road, about 110 m from the pod, and the clearing counts as discovered from the moment you see the flash.Run in the game: you arrive 112 m from the pod with the hot rod at the roadside
MediumA new game kept the crash site’s invisible partsAfter a new game the 14 fallen trunks and the pod still blocked the way, the six felled trees could be walked through, and the burnt grass stayed bare.Taking the site down removes the trunks’ and the pod’s collision, puts back the trees’ collision and grows the grass back.Run in the game: trunks 0, pod 0, trees 6 of 6, grass back to its first value
Medium-lowA grizzly’s knock-out on the ropeA bear already attacking could knock you out on the rope. You paid the ranger and lost the hours, and the next frame put you back on the route.A climb cannot start while a bear is after you, and a knock-out ends the climb first.Run in the game: see below
LowThe falling craft’s light left in the skyLeaving the game during the fall left the craft’s glow and trail (85 sprites) hanging in the sky of the next game.One clean-up for everything the fall puts in the sky, used when the fall ends and when the story is reset.Run in the game: 85 visible before, none after
LowQuitting to the title mid-climbThe next game started with the climbing hands and their hold rings on screen.Quitting ends the climb, and the climbing hands hide at once.Run in the game: off the rope and on foot at the title and after Continue
LowThe shower view running on a hidden tabSwitching to another tab of the observatory during the shower left it running unseen. At its end it closed whatever you were reading.The view stops when its eyepiece leaves the screen and starts again from the beginning when you come back.Run in the game: stopped on the Tonight tab; back on the telescope it played to the end and the craft fell
LowZib blinking across the map on ContinueZib was put at your side before you were moved to where you saved, so on the first frame it blinked across the map with a flash and a chirp.The story is restored after you are in place.Run in the game: no blink, 1.8 m from you
LowTopping out inside the summit blockOn Tundra Stroll and Ptarmigan Crack the spot where you stand after topping out was inside the summit block, so you appeared in the rock and were pushed out.The spot moves back from the lip only as far as you fit, clear of the summit block and the walls.Run in the game: see below
LowThe sample flake inside the summit blockThe loose flake you chip the granite sample from sat inside the summit block, half buried.It now lies on the first open corner of the stand.Run in the game: see below
LowThe coil’s explanation lostThe note about the coil waited 6.5 s and gave up for good if any screen was open then. After quitting to the title it could open over the title screen.It waits until the show is over and no screen is open, and is dropped when you quit.Run in the game: see below
Low, phonesA heavy trail behind the craftThe trail was 140 sprites, each its own draw call, about 100 at once for some 15 s at the climax: a likely stutter on a phone at the best moment. Its textures were never freed.Two point clouds, one of glow and one of smoke: two draw calls. Textures, materials and buffers are freed when the fall is over.Run in the game: the outburst script and its pictures
Low, phonesTwo sculptures at onceThe statue and Zib each took up to 3 ms a frame, and near the crash site, 255 m from the memorial, both could run in the same frame. One step of the sculpting could also overrun its share on a slow phone.One 3 ms budget a frame, shared by both, and steps about four times finer.Run in the game: the memorial and visitor scripts still finish both
LowThe cost of lowering offWhile lowering off, a ray was cast against every triangle of the tor each frame, with a new vector each time.Rays test one block at a time, only the blocks they pass near, once every 0.1 s, with no new objects.Run in the game: the climbing scripts
LowThe shower view’s clock running backwardA stale time stamp from the browser could run the show’s clock backward, so the show never ended. This was seen in the headless test browser.The clock never steps backward.Checked in the code
Found while writing this reportThe craft’s first frames cut offThe craft started exactly at the camera’s 9 km reach, so its first frames were not drawn.It now starts 8.5 km out.Checked in the code; the outburst script runs the fall
Found while writing this reportA wrong compass face in the codeA comment put Ptarmigan Crack on the west face of the big tor. Measured in the game it is the north face (342°), as the route board says.Comment corrected; this report uses the measured faces.Measured in the game

The review’s test script on the final build

  • Zib after a fast travel to the tors: 1.4 m from you.
  • On the rope: Drive there refused, with no time passed. A climb is refused with a bear about and allowed without. A knock-out on the rope leaves you on foot at Hotrod Landing with the climb over.
  • Quitting to the title mid-climb: off the rope, the climbing hands and the hold rings hidden. After Continue you are on foot.
  • Drive there to Starfall Clearing: you arrive 112 m from the pod, with the hot rod at the roadside.
  • A new game after the crash: trunks’ collision 0 (was 14), pod’s 0 (was 1), the trees’ 6 of 6, and the grass back to its first value.
  • The fall’s light: 4 objects in the sky mid-fall (the craft, its glow and the two clouds of the trail, where it was 85 sprites), and none after a reset.
  • The shower view: stopped when the Tonight tab replaced it. Back on the telescope it played to the end, the screen closed and the craft fell.
  • The top-out spots: all four on open rock. First Steps and Raven’s Roof are 1.6 m back from the lip, Tundra Stroll 1.0 m and Ptarmigan Crack 0.8 m. The sample flake is on open rock too.
  • The coil’s note: held while the map was open for 10 s, and shown when it closed.
  • Continue with Zib along: no blink, 1.9 m from you. An old save’s logs: 10 objectives caught up, $1,520, and the message naming them.

sections.title: What this report cannot show
sections.html:
• No real iPhone. The tap fix and the layout were tested in a desktop browser that pretends to be a touch screen at iPhone sizes. Safari on a real phone may still behave differently.
  • No frame rate. The test browser draws with software at about 4 seconds a frame. Smoothness can only be judged on a device. The draw call and triangle counts above are the best guide here.
  • The voice depends on the voices installed on each phone. A phone with only the basic voices will still sound flatter than one with an enhanced voice downloaded.
  • Some sources could not be read in full. The environment’s network rules turned away the command-line downloads from buffaloah.com, teslauniverse.com, en.wikipedia.org, mail.teslasociety.com and www.eia.gov. Those facts were checked through search results and the other pages listed. The hosts can be allowed under Network access in the environment’s settings, as described in the Claude Code on the web documentation.

sections.title: What would change this conclusion
sections.html:
The conclusion is that all eight requests are done and tested as far as a headless browser allows. These would change it:

  • The top-right buttons still do nothing on your iPhone. Then the dropped click was not the whole cause. The iOS version, the browser, and whether it happens on foot, driving or both would point to the rest.
  • RUN still covers the map. Then your screen size is one of the sizes not checked. A screenshot would give the exact size to add.
  • The announcer still sounds like a robot. The phone probably has no enhanced English voice. tapping Voice in the game’s Settings goes through what is there, and one can be downloaded in the iPhone’s Settings → Accessibility → Spoken Content → Voices.
  • The lag is still there. A recording from Safari’s Web Inspector on a Mac, with the phone connected, would show which part costs the time: the forest, the reflections or the shadows.
  • Climbing feels too hard or too easy with a thumb. Each kind of hold has one number for how fast it tires you, and the overhang has one more. They are quick to tune.
  • New research settles the Kappa Cygnids’ parent body. Then the telescope panel needs one line changed.
